title: Anyone's Sukkah, and a Mezuzah for the Inner Booth
subtitle: Closing the geometry, a potter's two nested booths, and two mnemonics covering every kind of pre-existing structure that can serve as a sukkah.
sources: Gemara text: Sefaria (William Davidson Edition). Structure and quiz questions 4-6 cross-checked against the Dafyomi Advancement Forum (dafyomi.co.il) quiz for Sukkah 8. Tosfos: dafyomi.co.il's "Point by Point Summary of Tosfos" (Yaakov Montrose, Kollel Iyun Hadaf).
before: 8a closed with the Caesarean judges proposing an area-based approach to Rabbi Yochanan's round-sukkah number. This amud opens by testing that approach against reality and finding it doesn't hold up either — leaving Rav Asi's answer from 8a as the one that sticks.

From there the daf turns to something much more down-to-earth: a potter's two nested booths (which one needs a mezuzah?), and then two memorized lists — GaNBaKh and RaKBaSh — covering every category of already-existing structure that can double as a kosher sukkah, gentile-built to guard-hut, provided it's actually roofed for shade.

flow.label: The Caesarean area-based approach, tested and rejected
flow.sub: predicts a circumference far larger than what's actually observed for a 16-perimeter square's circumscribing circle

flow.label: New topic: a potter's two nested booths — one inside the other
flow.sub: the potter lives in the inner one year-round; the outer one is just a shop-front

items.label: Inner booth
items.sub: needs a mezuzah — lived in year-round, so it's a real house; but not a valid sukkah, since living there isn't specifically for the festival

items.label: Outer booth
items.sub: no mezuzah — just a passage/shop-front, not a residence; but valid as a sukkah, since staying there during the festival is clearly for the mitzvah

flow.label: Gemara asks why the outer booth isn't at least a "gatehouse" of the inner one (which would need a mezuzah too)
flow.sub: answered: even the inner booth's own permanence is only borderline — not solid enough to extend obligation outward

flow.label: Two mnemonics of pre-existing structures that make valid sukkot
flow.sub: GaNBaKh (gentile / woman / animal / Samaritan) and RaKBaSh (shepherd / fruit-dryer / field-guard / produce-guard) — both lists, provided the roofing was built for shade

flow.label: Why two separate lists instead of one
flow.sub: each list's author finds his own cases more obviously valid (permanent structures vs. structures built by people actually obligated in the mitzvah), and adds the other list as the real novelty

flowCaption: One geometric approach falls, then two everyday questions: whose booth needs a mezuzah, and which found structures make a kosher sukkah.

opinions.claim: Of a potter's two nested booths, the inner one (lived in year-round) needs a mezuzah but isn't a valid sukkah; the outer one (a mere passage/shop-front) is a valid sukkah but doesn't need a mezuzah.
opinions.basis: Mezuzah requires a genuine, unambiguous residence; sukkah requires that dwelling there be recognizably for the festival's sake — the two booths satisfy opposite halves of that pair.

opinions.claim: A gentile's, a woman's, an animal's, or a Samaritan's booth is a valid sukkah, provided it's roofed for shade — and adds RaKBaSh's cases too.
opinions.basis: Finds his own list's cases more obviously valid, since they're all sturdy, permanent-feeling structures, even though none of their builders were obligated in the mitzvah.

opinions.claim: A shepherd's, fruit-dryer's, field-guard's, or produce-guard's booth is a valid sukkah, provided it's roofed for shade — and adds GaNBaKh's cases too.
opinions.basis: Finds his own list's cases more obviously valid, since their builders were all people actually obligated in the mitzvah, even though the structures themselves are seasonal, not permanent.

script.speaker: The Caesarean approach
script.quote: עִיגּוּלָא דְּנָפֵיק מִגּוֹ רִיבּוּעָא — רִבְעָא, רִיבּוּעָא דְּנָפֵיק מִגּוֹ עִיגּוּלָא — פַּלְגָא.
script.gloss: A circle inscribed in a square is a quarter smaller (by area); a square circumscribed by a circle is half the circle's size. On this logic, a circle of 24 amos circumference would circumscribe a 16-amos-perimeter square, matching Rabbi Yochanan exactly.

script.speaker: Gemara rejects it
script.quote: וְלָא הִיא, דְּהָא קָחָזֵינַן דְּלָא הָוֵי כּוּלֵּי הַאי.
script.gloss: But that's not so — we can directly observe that a circle circumscribing a 16-perimeter square doesn't actually come out that large. Rav Asi's answer from 8a stands as the accepted resolution.

script.speaker: New case
script.quote: שְׁתֵּי סוּכּוֹת שֶׁל יוֹצְרִים זוֹ לִפְנִים מִזּוֹ — הַפְּנִימִית אֵינָהּ סוּכָּה, וְחַיֶּיבֶת בִּמְזוּזָה. וְהַחִיצוֹנָה סוּכָּה, וּפְטוּרָה מִן הַמְּזוּזָה.
script.gloss: Two of a potter's booths, one inside the other: the inner one (lived in year-round) isn't a valid sukkah but does need a mezuzah; the outer one (a mere passage/shop-front) is a valid sukkah and is exempt from a mezuzah.

script.speaker: Gemara asks
script.quote: וְאַמַּאי? תִּהְוֵי חִיצוֹנָה כְּבֵית שַׁעַר הַפְּנִימִית, וְתִתְחַיֵּיב בִּמְזוּזָה!
script.gloss: Why isn't the outer booth at least obligated as the inner booth's "gatehouse"?

script.speaker: Answered
script.gloss: Because even the inner booth's own status as a permanent residence is only good enough to obligate itself in a mezuzah — not solid enough to extend that obligation outward to a gatehouse as well.

script.speaker: First mnemonic
script.quote: גַּנְבַּ״ךְ: סוּכַּת גּוֹיִם, סוּכַּת נָשִׁים, סוּכַּת בְּהֵמָה, סוּכַּת כּוּתִים סוּכָּה מִכׇּל מָקוֹם — כְּשֵׁרָה, וּבִלְבַד שֶׁתְּהֵא מְסוּכֶּכֶת כְּהִלְכָתָהּ.
script.gloss: GaNBaKh — the booth of a gentile, a woman, an animal, or a Samaritan — any of these is a valid sukkah, provided it's roofed in the standard way.

script.speaker: Gemara asks
script.gloss: What does "in the standard way" mean?

script.speaker: Rav Chisda answers
script.gloss: That it was built to provide the shade of a sukkah — its roofing has to actually function for that purpose, regardless of who built it or why.

script.speaker: Second mnemonic
script.quote: רַקְבַּ״שׁ: סוּכַּת רוֹעִים, סוּכַּת קַיָּיצִים סוּכַּת בּוּרְגָּנִין סוּכַּת שׁוֹמְרֵי פֵירוֹת, סוּכָּה מִכׇּל מָקוֹם — כְּשֵׁרָה.
script.gloss: RaKBaSh — the booth of a shepherd, a fig-dryer, a field-guard, or a produce-guard — same rule, same "roofed in the standard way" condition.

script.speaker: Why two separate lists
script.gloss: Each beraita adds the other's cases via its closing "of any sort" clause — but each Tanna starts from the cases that seem most obviously valid to him. GaNBaKh's cases feel solid because they're sturdy, permanent-style structures (even though none of their builders were obligated in the mitzvah). RaKBaSh's cases feel solid because their builders were obligated (even though the structures themselves are only seasonal).

tosfos.summary: Working out exactly what the Caesarean judges' "square inside a circle is half" claim actually means, and reconciling it with the earlier "quarter" rule (condensed here).

points.label: (b) Question on Rashi
points.he: ודבר תימה הוא זה מה ענין זה אצל זה
points.en: Rashi's reading (that this is about circumference) doesn't obviously connect the square's perimeter to the circle's circumference at all.

points.label: (c), (e)-(g) Tosfos's resolution
points.he: אלא יש לפרש ריבועא דנפיק מגו עיגולא פלגא... דהנך תרי מילי קיימי
points.en: The claim is about area, and specifically about a square inscribed inside a circle that is itself inscribed inside a larger square — the inner diamond-square is half the middle circle's area, which itself is a quarter less than the outer square. Both statements measure relative to the same outer square, and are mutually consistent once read that way.

tosfos.summary: Reconciling why a gatehouse generally IS obligated in mezuzah elsewhere, even though the potter's outer booth here isn't.

points.label: (b) Question
points.he: ותימה דבפ״ק דיומא אמרינן דממעטינן להו ממזוזה מדכתיב בית
points.en: Yoma (11b) excludes gatehouses from mezuzah entirely, from the word "house" implying a place built specifically for living — seemingly contradicting the assumption here that a gatehouse would otherwise be obligated.

points.label: (e) Answer
points.en: One exemption is Torah-level, the other only rabbinic — resolving the apparent tension between the two sugyot.

tosfos.summary: Why Samaritans (Kutim) appear on the GaNBaKh list alongside gentiles, women, and animals — none obligated in the mitzvah.

points.label: (a), (c) Explanation
points.he: כל הנך דקחשיב הכא... דלאו בני חיובא נינהו דקסבר גרי אריות הן
points.en: This sugya's view holds Samaritans converted out of fear rather than sincere conviction, so — on this opinion — they aren't halachically obligated in the mitzvah at all, same as the other names on the list.

points.label: (b)-(c) Reconciled with a contrary source
points.he: והא דאמר פ״ב דיבמות דאחד גרי אריות... הני מילי כשנתגיירו לגמרי
points.en: Elsewhere, fear-based converts are treated as valid converts generally — but Kutim specifically are described (Melachim II 17) as continuing to worship idols alongside God, which is a different, harsher case than an ordinary incomplete conversion.
